by Matt Hartley

Once cohost of the Linux action show.

I am not a technical Linux user. What makes me feel like that's ok is the fact that I break nothing and use freedom-respecting software. When I was on Windows, I would have to agree to some kind of terms when installing software and always check Users, control panel and app data for weird folders and other malware (there were plenty). I would say I felt like I had Windows under control. It all stopped when I completely switched to Linux. There is absolutely nothing to agree to when installing software on Linux and I didn't feel paranoid about sneaky files because it's all freedom-ware. The only time I broke something was when I dealt with some kind of non-free repo and its video driver. I went in with a Linux Live, copied what I needed, and re-installed Linux. Sure, I wish I could attach a couple hundred Linux commands under my belt for fun, productivity, and security. This is where something like this comes in as a learning tool. Anyways, I wish more things were automatic like hash checks and other security features but at the same time it would be cool to know how to manually verify a hash by copying one onto the clipboard and pasting it into the terminal. Because there aren't many reproducible resources, I'm forced to learn Linux very slowly. Other than the Home folder, I still have no idea what any of the folders are in the "Computer" button in "files". Not to worry, 10 years from now I will possibly get to know a few of them :)
Perhaps 'The Linux command line' can be helpful.
